schema.description: List Claude Code Remote sessions visible to the authenticated account. In bot contexts (e.g. Slack) this is a shared pool spanning many people, not just the human asking — pass mine: true to narrow to sessions started by the same account as the calling session. Returns session IDs, titles, statuses, and timestamps.

after_id.description: Pagination cursor: return sessions older than this session ID. Pass the last_id from a previous response to get the next page.

before_id.description: Pagination cursor: return sessions newer than this session ID. Pass the first_id from a previous response to get the previous page.

limit.description: Maximum number of sessions to return (default 20, max 100).

mine.description: Filter to sessions started by the same account as the calling session. Use this for 'my recent sessions' in shared bot contexts. In personal accounts the list is already scoped to you, so mine has no additional effect. Returns an error if the calling session has no resolvable originating account.

tags.description: Filter to interactive sessions carrying ANY of these tags. Cowork sessions are tagged "cowork-local" or "cowork-remote" and are excluded from the default (untagged) listing — pass those tags here to list them. Scheduled/trigger-fired runs are not included (same as the REST default). Max 16 tags. Only available to OAuth callers; returns an error for in-session and toolbox callers.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__list_triggers
tools.description: List Routines (scheduled triggers) owned by this account. Use it to find trigger IDs (trig_...) for update_trigger and delete_trigger. From a thread in a Slack channel, only Routines that fire into that thread's session are listed unless all_in_channel is true. Each entry has the Routine's id, name, cron_expression, run_once_at, enabled state, ended_reason, next_run_at, created_at, persistent_session_id, and last_run. last_run is the most recent recorded run {status, fired_at, finished_at, session_id}. It is absent when no run was recorded (e.g. never fired). For a Routine that wakes an existing session, last_run records that the wake was delivered (SUCCEEDED) or failed to deliver, not how the turn went, unless run tracking covers that session. A FAILED or repeatedly non-SUCCEEDED last_run means the Routine is not doing its job. ended_reason says why a disabled Routine is permanently disabled. suspension_reason (e.g. subscription_paused) marks a temporary hold that lifts when the owner's subscription resumes. Both empty means user-paused. One-shot Routines that already fired (e.g. delivered send_later reminders) and Routines moved to a project are hidden unless include_completed is true. Scheduled tasks stored locally by the Cowork desktop app are not listed.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__list_triggers
schema.description: List Routines (scheduled triggers) owned by this account. Use it to find trigger IDs (trig_...) for update_trigger and delete_trigger. From a thread in a Slack channel, only Routines that fire into that thread's session are listed unless all_in_channel is true. Each entry has the Routine's id, name, cron_expression, run_once_at, enabled state, ended_reason, next_run_at, created_at, persistent_session_id, and last_run. last_run is the most recent recorded run {status, fired_at, finished_at, session_id}. It is absent when no run was recorded (e.g. never fired). For a Routine that wakes an existing session, last_run records that the wake was delivered (SUCCEEDED) or failed to deliver, not how the turn went, unless run tracking covers that session. A FAILED or repeatedly non-SUCCEEDED last_run means the Routine is not doing its job. ended_reason says why a disabled Routine is permanently disabled. suspension_reason (e.g. subscription_paused) marks a temporary hold that lifts when the owner's subscription resumes. Both empty means user-paused. One-shot Routines that already fired (e.g. delivered send_later reminders) and Routines moved to a project are hidden unless include_completed is true. Scheduled tasks stored locally by the Cowork desktop app are not listed.

all_in_channel.description: Threads in a Slack channel only. If true, list every Routine in this channel, including other threads' and ones that start a new session each time they fire. Default false.

cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor from a previous response's next_cursor. Omit for the first page.

enabled.description: When set, only Routines whose enabled state matches. true hides fired one-shots, paused, and auto-disabled Routines; false shows only those. Omit for both.

include_completed.description: If true, also include one-shot Routines that have already fired (e.g. delivered send_later reminders) and Routines moved to a project. Default false — there can be thousands.

recurring.description: When set, filters by schedule shape: true keeps only cron-driven (recurring) Routines, false only one-shot and fire-only Routines. Omit for both.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__read_documentation
tools.description: The documentation for the machine and product this session runs in: a claude.ai cloud container and the settings around it (GitHub access, connectors, the environment's secrets, network access, setup script and installed tools, the session's limits, Remote Control). Read it whenever something about your container or environment comes up, whether it blocked you, you worked around it, or the person asked how to set it up. For example: a clone or push is refused, a service you need has no connected connector, an outbound host is denied, a command-line tool is missing, you need an API key. Read it rather than answering from memory because these settings move and get renamed faster than your training data, and a page says what is true now: the current steps, where in the product the person makes the change, and what you can do yourself. Reading a page also helps the person directly: in the Claude Code app they see a card with a button that takes them to that settings page, so they can fix it themselves while you carry on. Call it with no topic to list the pages and when each applies; call it with a topic to read that page. Read a page each time a different topic comes up; one read per topic is enough. It is read-only and needs no approval. It has nothing on bugs in the code you are working on.

service.description: The product the topic came up for, when there is one: must be one of this field's enum values. "other" stands for any product that is not among them. Omit it when no product is involved.

situation.description: Why you are reading the page. "blocked": you cannot finish what was asked. "worked_around": you finished another way. "asked": the person asked how to set this up, or you can see it will be needed.

topic.description: The page to read. Must be one of this field's enum values. Omit it to get the index of pages.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__register_repo_root
tools.description: Tell the session that a repo attached via add_repo has finished cloning, so its CLAUDE.md, skills, and plugins load on the next turn. Only call this immediately after a successful clone that add_repo instructed you to run — it returns a tool error for a repo that is not already in this session's sources.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__register_repo_root
schema.description: Tell the session that a repo attached via add_repo has finished cloning, so its CLAUDE.md, skills, and plugins load on the next turn. ## Claude_Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

## 4. What changed, and why each shape

### 4.1 The catchable throw, measured first

No interpreter native raised a Fortress exception before this rung (`grep -rn "FortressError\|getRootValue" ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue` finds only `Reflect.java:65-72`, which looks up constructors), and the brief asked for the route to be measured before the check could stay in Java. The path: a native method is applied by `MethodClosure.applyMethod` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/MethodClosure.java:85-86`) with no `catch`, so a `FortressError` thrown there reaches `Evaluator.forTry` (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:1323-1324`) unchanged, which hands the wrapped object to `handleException` to be matched by type. `Int.overflow()` (`glue/prim/Int.java:256-259`) builds it as `Evaluator.java:224-226` builds the try-atomic failure: a root value of the library, from `Driver.getFortressLibrary()` (whose own comment, `interpreter/Driver.java:61`, reads "Native code sometimes needs access to the library component wrapper"), wrapped with the one-argument `FortressError(FObject)` (`exceptions/FortressError.java:31-34`), which had no caller until now, since a native has no location or environment to give. **Measured: it arrives catchable.** Every `overflows(...)` assertion of the test passes, and its helper's only clause is `IntegerOverflow => true` (`IntSemanticsRungI.fss:6-12`), so the fallback of a Fortress-body `throw IntegerOverflow` was not needed. The interpreter's general mapping of other Java exceptions (`FunctionClosure.java:188-196` wraps any other `RuntimeException` of a native function in a `ProgramError`) is untouched, so the stop the brief names does not arise.

**Decision: the name is a `WellKnownNames` constant** (`compiler/WellKnownNames.java:86`, `integerOverflowException = "IntegerOverflow"`), beside the six exception names already there (`:80-85`), as `StringPrim.java:130-133` looks up `WellKnownNames.varargsFactoryName`. The alternative, a string literal in `Int.java`, would have kept the edit inside the manifest's file list; it was rejected because the interpreter's shape for "a library name the Java side looks up" is the constant at every site (five in `Evaluator.java`, one in `StringPrim.java`). The cost is one more 2012-tree file, on the `historical:` line.

### 4.2 GCD and LCM

`Int.gcd`'s zero case returned its other argument unnormalized (base `Int.java:253`); it now returns the magnitude (`Int.java:292`), and the function's existing convention that `Long.MIN_VALUE` stands for `2^63` (it negates and then shifts with `>>>`) is kept. `Int$Gcd` throws when the magnitude exceeds `Integer.MAX_VALUE` (`Int.java:134-140`), `Long$Gcd` when it is negative, i.e. `2^63` (`Long.java:148-154`). `LCM` on both widths goes through one new helper, `Int.lcm` (`Int.java:274-284`), which follows the compiled body (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:616-619`, `if (self = 0) OR (other = 0) then 0 else (|self| DIV (self GCD other)) DOT |other|`): zero first, then `|u / g| * |v|` by `Math.multiplyExact` (Java 8, and the JVM's own spelling of the check, as the batch record notes at `CLIMB-BATCH-3.5.md:36`), with the two operands whose magnitude has no `long` tested before `Math.abs`. `Int$Lcm` then range-checks to `int` (`Int.java:142-148`).

**Decision: `MIN GCD MIN` and `MIN LCM MIN` throw too.** The brief's list stops at `MIN GCD 0`, `0 GCD MIN`, `MIN LCM ±1` and `5 LCM MIN`; `MIN GCD MIN` (`2^31`, resp. `2^63`) and `MIN LCM MIN` are the same unrepresentable results reached with both operands at the minimum, measured wrapping on the base tree (`probes/IntSemProbe-before.txt:86`, `:89`, `:106`, `:109`), and the rule cannot be applied to half of them. `MIN LCM 0` is `0` (spec `:529`) and not a throw, although `MIN GCD 0` throws: the zero test comes before the divisor is computed, as in the compiled body.

`Int.rc` is untouched, as the brief requires (row 347 stays open). Its callers after this rung are `Int$Choose` (`Int.java:152`) and `Int$Pow` (`Int.java:225`); see section 9 on the brief's "two exponentiation callers".

### 4.3 The fixed widths, and how the count is read

Each of the four shift pairs gains one line before the existing one; `Int$LShift` (`Int.java:180-185`), for example, is `if (v < 0) return (v > -32) ? (u >> (int) -v) : (u >> 31);` followed by the original `((v & ~31) == 0) ? (u << (int) v) : 0`. The comparison with `-32` (`-64`) precedes the negation, so `Long.MIN_VALUE` is never negated. `NN32` and `NN64` shift right logically and saturate to `0` both ways (`NN32.java:183-195`, `UnsignedLong.java:184-196`).

**The `NN64` question, established.** `UnsignedLong$LShift` took its count through `UU2U`, whose `applyMethod` reads `y.getNN64()` (base `UnsignedLong.java:88-94`). Through that `long`, a negative count and a large unsigned one cannot be told apart: `FInt.getNN64` and `FLong.getNN64` return the signed value unchanged (`evaluator/values/FInt.java:36-39`, `FLong.java:37-40`), so a `ZZ32` count of `-1` and an `NN64` count of `2^64-1` both arrive as `-1L`, and `Long.MIN_VALUE` as a `ZZ64` count and `2^63` as an `NN64` count both arrive as `Long.MIN_VALUE`. **They can be told apart one step earlier, by the class of the count's value**, which is `FNN64` for an `NN64`. The same ambiguity sat in `Long$…` (`y.getLong()` of an `FNN64` is its raw bits) and in `BigNum`'s `ZL2Z`; it was harmless while every negative count saturated, and this rung's negative-count rule would have made it wrong (`-3 LSHIFT` an `NN64` count of `2^63` would have become a right shift, `-1` instead of `0`). So the count is read once, by `Int.shiftCount(FValue)` (`Int.java:261-272`): an `FNN64` of `2^63` or more as `Long.MAX_VALUE` (a count beyond every width), an `FBigNum` exactly when it fits a `long` and clamped to `Long.MIN_VALUE`/`Long.MAX_VALUE` when it does not (exact for every width, and for `ZZ`, whose values the JVM limits to `2^31-1` bits), anything else by `getLong()`. The guards are asserted at `IntSemanticsRungI.fss:73-76`.

Precedent for the shape: each natives file declares small abstract classes named for their Java types, with a shift-only one where the count's reading differs: `ZL2Z` in `Int.java:90-96` and `BigNum.java:102-108`, `NL2N` in `NN32.java:95-101`, each extended by the two shifts alone (`grep -n "extends ZL2Z\|extends NL2N"` finds only the shifts, plus the dormant `ZZ32.java`). Their `applyMethod` now calls `shiftCount`. `Long.java` and `UnsignedLong.java` had only the shared `LL2L`/`UU2U`, so each gains a shift-only twin, `LC2L` (`Long.java:104-110`) and `UC2U` (`UnsignedLong.java:96-102`), "C" for the count; the alternative, extending `NativeMeth1` directly as the `Pow` classes do (`Int.java:218-228`), was rejected to keep the four pairs one shape.

### 4.4 The unbounded ZZ

`BigNum$LShift` and `$RShift` (`BigNum.java:225-235`) call one helper, `shiftLeft(BigInteger, long)` (`BigNum.java:237-250`); `RShift` negates the count, mapping `Long.MIN_VALUE` to `Long.MAX_VALUE` first (both are beyond any `BigInteger`'s width, so the answer is the same). A negative count of magnitude up to `Integer.MAX_VALUE` is a `BigInteger.shiftRight`, a floor, as the spec's `shift` requires; beyond it the answer is `0` or `-1` by sign; zero shifted is zero; a positive count beyond `Integer.MAX_VALUE` on a nonzero value raises `IntegerOverflow`, and so does the JVM's own `ArithmeticException("BigInteger would overflow supported range")` for a count inside the `int` range whose result exceeds `BigInteger`'s limit (measured with a throwaway Java probe on JDK 25: `3 << 2147483645` succeeds with bit length `2147483647`, `3 << 2147483646` throws), caught at the call and translated.

**Decision: `IntegerOverflow`, catchable.** The brief left the exception to the rung. The alternatives were the raw `ArithmeticException` (uncatchable under `walk`, row 336's shape, and what the base tree already did for counts inside the `int` range), a `ProgramError` through `error(...)` (uncatchable, row 347's shape), or a new exception type. The spec's rule is that an integer result that does not fit throws `IntegerOverflow` (`opr-overview.tex:154-155`); `ZZ` has no width of its own but the JVM gives it one, and Pavol's principle is not to fight the JVM where it precludes an implementation; `IntegerOverflow` is the one exception the library has for "an integer result that does not fit". Translating the JVM's own check rather than predicting it keeps the limit the JVM's.

### 4.5 ZZ64.narrow

`Long$FromLong` is `(int) x` (`Long.java:248-252`), as `UnsignedLong$FromLong` (`UnsignedLong.java:240-243`) and `BigNum$ToZZ32` (`BigNum.java:282-285`) already were.

## 5. The `shift` declaration: the collision, and the renames the specification requires

The brief (`CLIMB-BATCH-3.5.md:46`): "The name is new at top level; the library's other shift is the array-origin dotted method (…), and a collision with it is a stop." The declaration is written as the brief says: `shift(self, k:AnyIntegral): ZZ` in `trait ZZ` of `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` (`:544`), and in the component `shift(self, k:AnyIntegral): ZZ = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.BigNum$LShift")` after `RSHIFT` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:885-886`). **Alone, it collided, not with the dotted method, but with every declaration of a parameter or local named `shift` in a component that sees the library**, and every `walk` run then failed before the program started. The five layers, measured in the first round with the declaration in place (the line numbers are those of the landed tree, one line below the base tree's in `FortressLibrary.fsi` and two below in `FortressLibrary.fss`, because the declaration and its body precede them):

- `probes/shift-collision-layer1.txt`: 12 × `Variable shift is already declared.`, at `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2081-2084` (the `Range` trait's `shiftLeft(shift: I)`, `shiftRight(shift: I)`, `opr <<(self, shift: I)`, `opr >>(self, shift: I)`) and `Library/RangeInternals.fsi:194-195`, `:263-264`, `:323-324`, `:431-432`.
- With those twelve renamed (to `amount`, in a trial only), `probes/shift-collision-layer2.txt`: 6 more, at `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3670-3673` and `:3688-3689`; then `probes/shift-collision-layer3.txt`: 30 more in `Library/RangeInternals.fss`, from `:454` to `:1357`; then `probes/shift-collision-layer4.txt`: `Library/List.fss:311`, a local `shift = start - firstUsed`; then `probes/shift-collision-layer5.txt`: clean (its two errors are the probe program's own, below).

The rule is the disambiguator's `checkForShadowingVar` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/disambiguator/ExprDisambiguator.scala:745-763`): a variable may not shadow any variable or function in scope, and an imported api's functional methods are in scope in every importer. It is not peculiar to `shift`: `probes/ShadowEven.fss` binds a parameter `even` and a local `numerator`, both functional methods of the library's `ZZ` today, and on the unedited library gets `Variable even is already declared.` and `Variable numerator is already declared.` (`probes/ShadowEven.txt`). The specification makes the collision real at least inside the library's own component: "It is also a static error for multiple declarations with overlapping reaches to declare the same name in the same namespace unless the declarations are overloaded or one declaration shadows the other" (`Specification/basic/declarations.tex:426-432`); a parameter is not among the declarations that may shadow ("No other shadowing is permitted in a Fortress program", `:533`, after the list at `:476-529`); and "The reach of a functional method declaration is the component containing that declaration" (`:435-436`), which takes in `FortressLibrary`'s own `Range` trait. A parameter's own reach is its functional declaration (`:459-461`), so the reaches overlap. For the importing components (`RangeInternals`, `List`, a user's program), "the reach of any top-level declaration (including any imported declaration) is the component containing (or importing) that declaration" (`:454-456`), which is the reading the implementation, shared by both paths, enforces.

**What it cost.** The landed edit is the first round's trial patch unchanged (`probes/route-i-trial-patch.txt`, applied with `git apply` in commit `fafc4eb75`): the declaration and its body (one line in the api, two in the component), and 49 declarations of a parameter or local named `shift` renamed to `amount`: 4 in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` (`:2081-2084`), 6 in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` (`:3670-3673`, `:3688-3689`), 8 in `Library/RangeInternals.fsi` (`:194-195`, `:263-264`, `:323-324`, `:431-432`), 30 in `Library/RangeInternals.fss` and 1 in `Library/List.fss` (`:311`), 71 changed lines over the five files with the uses in their bodies. After it, `grep -rnw shift` over `Library/*.fss`, `Library/*.fsi` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/*.fs[si]` shows only the array-origin dotted declarations (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1294`, `:1317`, `:1337`, `:1417`, `:1447`, and two more the brief's list does not name, `Array2`'s at `:1557` and `Array3`'s at `:1688`, all inside trait declarations) with their component bodies and one call (`FortressLibrary.fss:1757`), the new declaration and body, and six comments in `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. The renames change no type and no declaration a gated test names (`shiftLeft`, `shiftRight`, `<<` and `>>` keep their names and types), and the renamed parameters are positional, not the keyword-parameter declarations of `Specification/basic/declarations.tex:243-244`, so no call site names them. Measured on the landed tree: the test prints `PASS` (`test-after.txt`); `tests/subArray.fss`, the corpus's one caller of an array's `.shift(`, and the tests of the renamed `Range` and `ArrayList` code pass under the harness (`probes/harness-shift-landed.txt`, section 8), so the dotted method does not collide, as `declarations.tex:416-425` predicts for a name after a `.`; the checker count stays 103 (`probes/checker-count-after-shift.txt`). It makes `shift` a name no `walk` program may bind, as `even` and `numerator` already are; section 8 measures that cost at zero files.

**Why it landed.** The first round held the item as the brief's stop and offered Pavol four options (a dotted `x.shift(k)`, another spelling, leaving it undeclared, or this patch). `JUDGE.md` section 2 ruled that the brief's stop names a collision with the array-origin dotted method, which does not occur, and section 3 that the specification settles both the declaration (`basic-integers.tex:695-702`) and the renames (`declarations.tex:426-436`, `:454-461`, `:533`), so that only this patch is consistent with both the specification and Pavol's decision.

## 6. Two further defects found, and repaired

### 6.1 A `ZZ` count crashed every fixed-width shift

Every fixed-width shift declares its count `AnyIntegral` or `ZZ64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:637-638` on `Integral`, and the overrides), and `AnyIntegral` comprises `ZZ`, but the natives read the count with `getLong()`, which on an `FBigNum` throws unconditionally (`evaluator/values/FBigNum.java:48-50`, "might not fit in ZZ64"): `widen(3) LSHIFT big(widen(3))` ended the run with `ProgramError: Value 3 might not fit in ZZ64.` (`probes/run-enders-before.txt`, case 7; a `ZZ32` receiver reaches `Long$LShift` by dispatch, case 8). `Int.shiftCount` reads it exactly, and the two now answer `24` and `-1` (`probes/run-enders-after.txt`). **Decision: repaired here**, because the count reader this rung needed anyway is the fix; the alternative was a ledger row. Home 1: `IntSemanticsRungI.fss:81-82`, cited to the declaration `FortressLibrary.fss:637`.

### 6.2 The `ZZ` natives read an `NN64` of `2^63` or more as negative

`BigNum.toB`, the receiver and argument conversion of every `BigNum$…` native, fell through to `BigInteger.valueOf(x.getLong())` for an `FNN64` (base `BigNum.java:41-49`), so `NN64 2^63 + ZZ 0` was `-9223372036854775808` and `NN64 2^63 = ZZ 2^63` was `false` (`probes/IntSemProbe-before.txt:66-68`), where `ZZ` "encompasses all finite integers" (`basic-integers.tex:15-16`). The same misreading made a `ZZ` shift by an `NN64` count of `2^63` a no-op (`:63-64`). `toB` now converts an `FNN64` exactly, in the spelling of the compiled world's `simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.makeZZfromNN64` (`nativeHelpers/simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.java:117-119`; `BigNum.java:46-48`). **Decision: repaired here**, because the `shift` declaration's route needs it and it is one branch in a file this rung edits; it changes the answer of any `ZZ` operator reached with an `NN64` operand of `2^63` or more, from wrong to right, and nothing else. ## 7. The gated test that relied on the old LCM

The regression subset (section 8) turned up one red: `tests/RangePrototype.fss`, `FAIL: a dumpShow[\ZZ32\]: RightScalarRange(2,1)==...-2,-1,0,1,2] =/= a dumpShow[\ZZ32\]: LeftScalarRange(2,-1)==[2,1,0,-1,-2...;` for `(spec, curr) match for OpenScalarRange(1)==...o,o+1... and LeftScalarRange(2,-1)` (`probes/harness-regression-1.txt:6-8`). ## 1. Finding 1, the refusal ground: upheld

**What is true.** `BigNum.shiftLeft` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/BigNum.java:237-250`) bounds the count at `:243` (`if (v > Integer.MAX_VALUE) throw Int.overflow();`) and then calls `u.shiftLeft((int) v)` inside a `try` at `:244-249`, translating the `ArithmeticException`. The JVM's `BigInteger.shiftLeft` allocates the shifted magnitude before its range check throws, so for `3 << 2147483647` about 268 MB is asked for first. The interpreter's launcher gives the JVM `-Xmx256m` unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set (`bin/fortress:28-29`), and the harness gives it 768 MB (root `build.xml:131`, `junitMem`, used by the `junit` task's `maxmemory` at `:1181`; `probes/harness-one.sh` copies that as `-Xmx768m`). Measured by the skeptic on the landed tree: under `bin/fortress` with `JAVA_FLAGS` unset the gated test dies at `IntSemanticsRungI.fss:93` with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` (`probes/skeptic/test-default-heap.txt:1-3`), and prints `PASS` without that line (`probes/skeptic/test-default-heap-no93.txt`); the same shift is `THROWS IntegerOverflow` at 768m and 4g (`probes/skeptic/SkBigAlloc.txt:6-10`) and an `OutOfMemoryError` at 256m (`:1-4`).

**Why it is refusal-grade.** Three reasons, any one enough. `record.md` FACTS line 2 (`record.md:10`) and `REPORT.md` section 4.4 (`REPORT.md:71-73`) claim an unrepresentable left shift raises "a catchable `IntegerOverflow`", unconditionally; it does so only above the launcher's heap, and a claim that holds only under the shared prefix's `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g ..."` is not a fact about the tree. An `OutOfMemoryError` is a `java.lang.Error` that no Fortress `catch` and no harness expected-failure sees, so the gated assertion `:93` is a red at the tree's own default that the gate cannot show. And a runtime that allocates 268 MB to learn that a shift does not fit, when the answer is one `bitLength()`, is the wrong shape for a language whose specification says overflow "throws an `IntegerOverflow`" (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`, read with `:140-170`).

**The repair, and why it is exact.** The skeptic's one line after `:243`, `if (u.abs().bitLength() + v > Integer.MAX_VALUE) throw Int.overflow();`, trialled in a scratch overlay (`probes/skeptic/fix-trial-patch.txt`), makes the unmodified test print `PASS` at `-Xmx256m` (`probes/skeptic/fix-trial-default-heap.txt`). It is exact by the worker's own measurement in `REPORT.md:71`: `3 << 2147483645` succeeds with bit length 2147483647 and `3 << 2147483646` throws, which is `2 + 2147483645 <= Integer.MAX_VALUE < 2 + 2147483646`; the JVM's limit is a magnitude of `Integer.MAX_VALUE` bits, and `u.abs().bitLength()` is the magnitude's bit length (for a negative power of two, `u.bitLength()` alone is one less, so `abs()` is not decoration). Two things the repair worker must keep:

- `:243` stays, and stays first. `Int.shiftCount` (`Int.java:261-272`) clamps an `NN64` count of `2^63` or more and a `ZZ` count beyond a `long` to `Long.MAX_VALUE`; without `:243` ahead of it, `bitLength + v` overflows the `long`, the precheck falls through, and `(int) v` is `-1`, a silent right shift. The existing assertion `IntSemanticsRungI.fss:95` (`bigThree LSHIFT twoTo63` overflows) is the guard on that order.
- The `try`/`catch` at `:244-249` stays as a backstop. The precheck's exactness rests on a JDK-internal constant (`BigInteger.MAX_MAG_LENGTH`), which is the JDK's to change; the catch costs nothing and keeps the translation if the constant ever moves.

**What the worker got wrong here, and what right.** `REPORT.md:73` took a decision, "translating the JVM's own check rather than predicting it keeps the limit the JVM's", without measuring at the launcher's heap; the shared prefix's `JAVA_FLAGS` hid the failure, and the base tree fails the same way (the base's `u.shiftLeft((int) v)` at base `BigNum.java:224` is the same call), so this is not a regression but it is the rung's claim. Everything else in section 4.4 is right and stays: the negative count of any size, zero shifted, the count beyond `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, and the choice of `IntegerOverflow` (`opr-overview.tex:154-155`).
